2. The appreciation of this Rule will be best done if the facts of this case are gone into which have a long history. The petitioner claims to be a national of Bangladesh and has been living in this country for generations being born at 23/1 Dhakeswari Road, within the police station of Lalbagh in the District of Dacca on 4.10.1928. He passed his matriculation examination from Nabakumar Institute at Dacca in the year 1948 being a student of that Institute althrough but he did not prosecute further studies, and started managing and performing pujas of Dhakeswari Mondir as his parents were the Sebaiet of that Dhakeswari Deity. The petitioner besides being the owner of 7 Orphanage Road has got other landed properties in Dacca and a sweetmeat shop at 8 Orphanage Road situated within the compound of Dhakeswari Temple and has a Municipal license to that effect. 

 3. It is further alleged in the petition that over the said sweetmeat shop fin has dispute with his co-sharer one Hem Chandi Chakrabvarty who has been trying to harrass the petitioner put him into various difficulties and has instituted several cases against him. The said Hem Chandra Chakravarty has been alleging that the petitioner is an Indian National and has unauthorized entered into the territory of Bangladesh and over this several cases have been instituted, one of which is pending decision before the Magistrate, 1st Class in Dhaka. A long history of legal battle which is waged by the petitioner against various orders passed by the authorities has been given in this petition which we need not recount here in view of the fact that these have been fully traced and discussed in a judgment delivered by this Bench in Criminal Revision No. 1577 of 1974, the judgment having been delivered on 1st of April, 1975. 

 4. The petitioner moved several other applications before this court. These are Petition No. 651 of 1974, Petition No. 681 of 1974 and Petition No. 10 of 1974. These 3 petitions, namely, Petition Nos. 651, 681 and 10 of 1974 were disposed of by a judgment of this Court delivered by K. Hossain and S. M. Hussain, JJ., on 19.8.74 and 3.9.74. Another application was filed challenging an order passed under Rule 5 of the Emergency Powers Rules which terminated in favour of the petitioner by a judgment of this Court delivered by A. T.M. Masud and A. I. Chowdhury, JJ., on 20.5.75 in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 181 of 1974. 

 6. The impugned order was purportedly passed under the Foreigners Order 1951 by the Civil authority on 1.7.75 and was served on the petitioner on 4.7.75 while the petitioner was detained in Dacca Central Jail. It may be mentioned in this connection that by the judgment in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 181 of 1974 their Lordships Masud and A. I. Chowdhury, JJ., declared the order passed under the Emergency Powers Rules detaining the petitioner null and void and their lordships in the concluding portion of the judgment directed "Bishal Deo Tewary, the petitioner before us, to be set at liberty forthwith" after making the Rule absolute. This order was passed on 20. 5. 75. The petitioner, however, was not released in pursuance of this judgment and order of their Lordships and yet another order was served on him on 31. 5. 75 under clause 15 of the Foreigners Order 1951, while the petitioner was still detained in jail. It may be seen that this order was passed on 31. 5. 75, that is, 11 days after the judgment of this Court directing the petitioner before us "to be set at liberty forthwith". The order of this Court was not carried out instead another order was passed purporting to detain the petitioner before us under clause 15 of the Foreigners Order 1951 (Annexure 'A'). As a result, another application was filed by the petitioner, before this Court on 9. 6. 75 being Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 65 of 1975. This order passed under clause 15 was rescinded by the same civil authority on 27. 6. 75 (Annexure 'B') and in that order dated 27. 6. 75 the petitioner was directed to be released from custody 'forthwith'. It will, however, appear that he was not released till 4. 7. 75 on which date he was served with the order purported to be passed under clause 11 of the Foreigners Order 1951 dated 1 7. 75. We have already noted that this order No. 5 dated 1.7.75 was served on the petitioner while he was still under detention in the Dacca Central Jail on 4. 7. 75. The impugned order reads as follows: 

 8. Affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondent No. 2 and on our direction subsequently an affidavit-in-opposition has been sworn by the Home Secretary himself in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 82 of 1975 which arose in pursuance of this case. 

 10. Mr. Afzal, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the State has made two submissions firstly that this petition under section 491 of the Code is not maintainable because the petitioner at the time of filing this petition was not in the custody of any authority private or public. The second contention is that the Government in the facts of this case is authorized to serve an order under clause 11 of the Foreigners Order 1951. 

 12. In the instant case the impugned order purports firstly to force the petitioner to reside within the jurisdiction of Sutrapur Police Station which is not his residence. The order itself notes that the petitioner's residence in Dacca is at Dhakeswari Mondir. It, therefore, forces the petitioner to leave his residence and reside in some other place, which is not even within the police station of his residence. Secondly, the petitioner has to inform the officer-in-charge of Sutrapur police station to address of the petitioner and thirdly, the petitioner could move out of his residence only on prior report to the officer-in-charge of the said police station. In spite of the learned Deputy Attorney-General's contention that this order by no means shows that the petitioner is under the custody of the officer-in-charge of the Sutrapur Police Station, it cannot be presumed that the said officer-in-charge must be made for such reasons as are only known to the executive authority aware of his movements, the learned Deputy Attorney-General has further submitted that unless it could be shown that the petitioner was in actual custody of the officer-in-charge of the said police station the application is not maintainable. 

 15. The impugned order dated 1.7.75 is in our opinion for all practical purposes an order which is an internment order passed by the authority concerned and as such jurisdiction under section 491 of this Court is attracted. Reference may be made to a Full Bench decision of the Lahore Bench of the West Pakistan High Court in the case of Choudhury Mohammad Anwar Vs. The Government of West Pakistan, P.L.D. 1963 Lah. 109. Chief Justice Manzur Qadir in dealing with the aspect of internment order observed (at page 126, para (10) as follows : 

 "Having had the advantage of bearing learned arguments and examining a large number of decided cases, that were most ably analyzed at the Bar, I have come to the conclusion that the restrictions placed on the movements of the petitioners in these cases do amount to their being in custody. It seems to me that the essence of custody is that there should be a lack of freedom to move about where and when one pleased coupled with a physical power immediately available to prevent an attempt at breakings the restrictions imposed as distinguished from the power subsequently to punish for a breach of these restrictions. If a person has been ordered that he must not go beyond certain boundaries, but there is no physical impediment or threat of physical force to ensure that he does not go outside those boundaries there would in my opinion be no confinement and no custody, even though that person may be liable to be punished in due course of law if he did go out. On the other hand, if he is told that be must not go beyond those boundaries and be sees or is told that if he did, physical force would be available to prevent him doing so, there would in my opinion, then be no difference of kind between his confinement or custody and that of a person confined in jail, though there would, of course, be a difference of degree". 

 The order of internment in this case is slightly different from the order in Pakistan case, but the principle that we have tried to lay down get support from the principle laid down by the Lahore High Court. 

 17. This Order, in our opinion, could only be passed in the case of a person who admittedly a foreigner and has entered into the territory of Bangladesh as foreigner without the necessary permission of the authority concerned. We have taken this view particularly because when there is an entry of a foreigner without necessary permission an order could be passed under clause 14 of the Order which reads as follows: 

 "14. Where an order is made in the case of any foreigner directing that he shall not remain in (Pakistan) or where a foreigner is refused permission to enter (Pakistan) or has entered (Pakistan) without permission, the (Central) Government, may, if it thinks fit, apply any money or property of the foreigner in payment of the whole or part of the expenses of or incidental to the voyage from (Pakistan) and the maintenance until departure of the foreigner and his dependents, if any". 

 18. The restrictions sought to be imposed upon the movement of the petitioner under the Foreigners Order, in our opinion, constitutes a clear fraud on the Foreigners Order in the peculiar facts and circumstances of this case, because of the legal battle that is being waged by this petitioner against the executive authority for securing his liberty since 1972. The order, therefore, amounts to an abuse of the powers given to the executive by the Legislature and hence we hold that such order could be challenged in an application under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. This view is further supported by the fact that a person served with an order under clause 11 of the Order is left without any legal remedy provided by the Order itself and as such is contradictory to the concept of criminal jurisprudence.
